issue_context.title: Scheduler loop loses time
issue_context.body:
https://github.com/facebook/osquery/blob/483fbbb594fe7172d6c008e1a018eb9c107ba99e/osquery/dispatcher/scheduler.cpp#L154

The loop variable used by the scheduler is supposed to be the time, but it tracks time imprecisely and generally loses time. This is because `i` is incremented by the loop, and the loop generally runs for *at least* one second (the `pauseMillis(1000)` call plus however long any queries take to run. (The slower the query, the further behind the loop will fall.)

This likely doesn't matter much for detection scenarios, but I've been using osquery for more performance-monitoring cases, which has meant more frequent (and sometimes higher-overhead) queries that can result in larger slips. I'd prefer to see logic where on each run through the loop it would execute (once) any queries that were scheduled to run at least once since the last start-of-loop timestamp. That way a single slow query could delay another query scheduled during the same time window, but would not have a cascading impact on other queries.
comments: Hi @jkeljo, yeah it looks you're correct, but I'm not sure I follow the solution you're proposing. Could you please explain?

Right, osquery intervals are loosely based on time. And time is a seed as to where to start incrementing.

> This likely doesn't matter much for detection scenarios

Right!

> but would not have a cascading impact on other queries

I think real-time query intervals are doable. You can use a `rt-interval` or a boolean `realtime: True` to distinguish.

Oh, forgot to mention... if the main loop is written that way, it's probably not just queries, but various kinds of tasks. (E.g. the current loop has some logic to update the decorators every 60 seconds; that could just be another task with a 60-second interval.)
Hi @jkeljo , does PR #4393 solve this problem? Is here something else to do in terms of this issue?
I think #4393 is good enough for now.

review_comments: Why not use std::priority_queue here, it will clearly show intension here + will help avoid cases when someone add value without std::push_heap.

You are right, using `std::priority_queue` easy to read and understand. But this approach has a defect. We are not able to pull out the top element from the queue by [moving](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/value_category) it. We can only copy the [top](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/priority_queue/top) and remove it by [pop](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/priority_queue/pop). But this is two more copies of task object, even thought the task copying is pretty cheap for now. We can avoid it just using the raw interface of [heap](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/algorithm/make_heap) from std. Does it make sense?
Forget to mention, lambda inside the task can be mutable, so it not a good idea to copy mutable lambda.
